title.en: Tales by dots and lines: mean as balance and interpreting data

text.en: On a see-saw, children of different weights balance at one point. The mean of a data set also acts as a balance point.

The mean is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values, and the median is the middle value when the data is sorted.
For 3 and 7 the mean is 5, and for 8 and 9 the mean is 8.5, which is always halfway between two numbers.
On a dot plot the mean is the balance point: the total distance of values below the mean equals the total distance above it.
For 10, 10, 11 and 17 the mean is 12, and the distances below (2 + 2 + 1) equal the distance above (5).
The mean is the only point with this equal-distance property, so it is a fair centre.
An outlier is a value far from the others; it drags the mean towards itself but changes the median very little.
A dot plot shows every value as a dot, so we can see clusters, gaps and outliers.
A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time, and steep parts show rapid change.
To read data well, look at the title, axes, scale, and units before drawing conclusions.
Choose the mean for fairly even data and the median when outliers exist.

problem.en: Find the mean and median of 4, 6, 6, 9, 20. Which is better?

text.en: Median = the middle value of the sorted data = 6.
The outlier 20 pulls the mean up, so the median 6 shows the typical value better.

prompt.en: Why is the mean called a balance point?

requiredIdeas.en: Distances below the mean sum to the same as distances above it.
Like a see-saw, the data balances there.

commonMisconceptions.en: The mean is always the middle value.

points.en: Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle value.
The mean balances distances on a dot plot.
Outliers affect the mean more than the median.
